title: Updated public tree by-law and higher parking fines
subtitle: Administrative penalties for parking violations, tree compensation rules, and a rental replacement by-law update.
overview: The Community and Infrastructure Services Committee recommended that Council repeal and replace the public tree by-law, which covers city-owned trees on city land. The new version tightens protection around existing trees during construction, adds a scaled removal and compensation program, and sets new administrative fines. Staff said it supports the city's tree canopy targets, and the committee backed it {{vote:m2}}.
The committee also recommended raising penalty fines for parking violations under the Administrative Monetary Penalty System {{vote:m1}}. This was handled as a consent item without discussion.

The committee also received an information report on the first year of the Rental Replacement By-law. Staff explained that tenants displaced by redevelopment return at the rent they were paying, and that six applications are expected. For residents, the changes mean clearer rules and higher costs for removing public trees, higher parking fines if Council adopts them, and ongoing protection for existing tenants.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended repealing Chapter 690 and replacing it with the proposed Public Tree By-law, with staff directed to carry out education, enforcement and monitoring.
The same motion recommended approving the administrative penalty fines for the Public Tree By-law set out in Attachment B of the staff report.
The committee recommended authorizing the Clerk to update Chapter 690 of the Municipal Code to reflect the new by-law.
The committee recommended approving Schedule A under the Administrative Monetary Penalty System to increase penalty fines for parking violations.

debate: Councillors asked how fines would deter removals. Staff said a fine alone cannot stop someone from removing a tree. Compensation pays for replanting, and more serious cases can be prosecuted in court with a much higher maximum penalty.

Several councillors raised delays in replacing boulevard trees. Staff said replacement typically takes up to two years, because stump removal needs utility locates that can take weeks and planting happens only in spring and fall. A stumping backlog has been cleared, and staff expect faster turnaround.

A councillor asked how the by-law applies to the city's own projects. Staff said most of its effect falls on internal teams, such as stormwater and park work. They have piloted it for several months without significant problems.

Staff explained that the city did not create a permit system for public trees because neighbouring municipalities gave poor reviews of theirs. A separate review of private tree rules is expected to return to Council later this year.

On the rental replacement update, a councillor asked about developments missing from the report. Staff said no application had been received for one site. They said the report covers only the cases in active discussion.
